name: Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station
description: Three-unit pressurized-water-reactor nuclear plant west of Phoenix, cooled with treated municipal wastewater. Its figures are EIA-860 nameplate capacity, 2024 net generation, reported cooling-water use, site area, staffing and the reported construction cost.
headline: 4,210 MW nuclear (3 × PWR) · Arizona

referenceSite.name: Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station, Wintersburg, Maricopa County, Arizona

footprintProvenance.note: [S6] POWER magazine (Nov 2015): the plant is located on 4,000 acres of desert about 50 miles west of Phoenix. 4,000 acres × 4,046.856 m²/acre = 16,187,424 m². This is the whole site, including the 80-acre storage reservoir and the evaporation ponds, not only the power blocks.

power.technology: Three Combustion Engineering System 80 PWRs with steam turbines (in service 1986, 1986, 1988); three mechanical forced-draft cooling towers on treated municipal effluent

provenance.note: [S1] GridInfo, republishing the 2025 EIA-860 report for plant 6008: three generators of 1,403.2 MW nameplate each, so ratedOutputKw = 4,209,600 kW. [S7] (EIA Electricity Data Browser table) and [S2] Pinnacle West: 2024 NET generation 32,388,118 MWh ÷ 8,784 h (2024 is a leap year) = 3,687,171.9 kW, entered as averageOutputKw. Gross generation could not be confirmed, so output is the net figure: the station's own electricity use is already deducted from it, and averageDemandKw is set to 0 so that own use is counted exactly once (inside the net figure), not because the plant uses no electricity. [S6] gives the technology: Combustion Engineering System 80 PWRs, and three mechanical forced-draft cooling towers, one per unit.

water.basis: Treated municipal wastewater from Phoenix-area cities, further treated on site, used as cooling-tower make-up; blowdown goes to on-site evaporation ponds (no water output)

provenance.note: [S4] Associated Press (May 2022): the plant uses about 65 million gallons of treated wastewater every day, more than 23 billion gallons a year. 65 MGD × 157.725491 = 10,252 m³/hour (a daily average spread over 24 h). Cross-checks: [S3] APS says Palo Verde recycles more than 20 billion gallons of wastewater a year, a lower bound. [S5] the 2010 agreement with Phoenix, Mesa, Tempe, Scottsdale and Glendale allows up to 80,000 acre-feet a year through 2050; this is an allocation cap, not actual use. [S6] says the effluent is further treated at the on-site Palo Verde Water Reclamation Facility and that cooling-tower blowdown is discharged to evaporation ponds, so water output is left empty.

[S3] APS: the plant has 2,500 full-time employees, used for staffingRequired. APS adds that 900 to 1,000 contractors are employed during the planned refuelling outages held twice a year; they are not included. The older POWER (2015) figure of about 3,000 workers [S6] is not used. No source states a maximum on-site capacity, so capacity is left unknown.

costs.priceBasis: reported construction cost in nominal USD; construction ran 1976–1988 and POWER gives no price year (Wikipedia, citing Shepherd 1989, labels it 1986 USD)

provenance.note: [S6] POWER magazine (2015): Palo Verde began construction in 1976 and was completed in 1988 at a cost of $5.9 billion. The figure has not been inflated or converted. [S7] Wikipedia labels the figure 1986 USD, citing Shepherd (1989). No source read states an operating cost or the effluent price. APS's $130 million a year of purchases from Arizona businesses [S3] is not a total operating cost, so it is not used.

name: Mesquite Generating Station
description: Natural-gas combined-cycle power plant (two 2x1 blocks: four gas turbines, two steam turbines) at Arlington, Arizona, in commercial operation since 2003. power.technology: Natural-gas combined cycle, 2 x (2 gas turbines + 1 steam turbine), dry low-NOx burners + SCR

name: Agua Caliente Solar Project
description: A 290 MW utility-scale photovoltaic plant in Yuma County, Arizona, using First Solar thin-film cadmium telluride modules on fixed-tilt mounts across about 2,400 acres. Output figures are EIA-reported 2024 net generation; land, water and staffing come from the DOE environmental assessment and loan announcement, DC capacity from EIA-860M, and cost from a co-owner's SEC filing.

name: Claude "Bud" Lewis Carlsbad Desalination Plant
description: The largest seawater reverse-osmosis desalination plant in the United States, on Agua Hedionda Lagoon in Carlsbad, California, supplying the San Diego County Water Authority since late 2015. The figures describe the plant at its typical 50 million gallons per day (MGD) output.
headline: 50 MGD seawater RO desalination · California

referenceSite.name: Claude "Bud" Lewis Carlsbad Desalination Plant, Carlsbad, CA

footprintProvenance.note: [S2] IDE Americas (EPC/O&M contractor), 2015 deck: 'Footprint: 6 acres (24,000 m²)' and 'Plant footprint - 6 acres'. 6 acres x 4,046.856 = 24,281.1 m². IDE's own rounded conversion is 24,000 m². This is the plant site only, not the 10-mile product pipeline or the lagoon.

power.technology: Seawater reverse osmosis: dual-media and cartridge filtration, 14 RO trains (14,000 membranes), 4 high-pressure pumps with PX pressure-exchanger energy recovery, remineralisation

provenance.note: averageDemandKw: [S3] Voutchkov (Jan 2009), total annual energy use of 246,156 MWh/yr at an annual average plant production of 50 MGD (13.5 kWh per 1,000 gallons of drinking water). 246,156,000 kWh / 8,760 h = 28,100 kW continuous average (operatingHoursPerDay = 24). This is a pre-operation design figure, not metered consumption. technology: [S2] process block diagram and 'Key Technical Parameters': 14 RO trains, 14,000 RO membranes, 4 high-pressure pumps, 8 ERI trains with 168 PX300Q pressure exchangers, re-hardening (post-treatment). peakDemandKw is left blank because no source gives a metered peak or a connection rating.

water.basis: Open seawater intake on Agua Hedionda Lagoon (Pacific Ocean); SWRO at about 50% recovery; brine (about twice seawater salinity) discharged to the ocean

provenance.note: outputM3PerHour: [S1] SDCWA says the plant 'is capable of delivering more than 50 million gallons of fresh, desalinated drinking water per day'. [S4] San Diego Regional Water Board gives 'an average daily flow of 50 million gallons per day (MGD)'. 50 MGD x 157.725491 = 7,886.27 m³/h. inputM3PerHour: [S1] SDCWA says 'On a typical day, the Carlsbad plant uses 100 million gallons of seawater'. 100 MGD x 157.725491 = 15,772.55 m³/h. Recovery in basis: 50/100 = 50% (derived); [S2] gives ~52% at design. Brine salinity is from [S4].

staffingRequired: [S2] IDE Americas 2015 says 'IDE O&M Team in Place: January of 2015 (38 employees)'. This is the operations and maintenance team at commissioning and is the only staffing figure found. capacity is left blank because no source states a maximum number of workers on site at one time. The 2,400 construction-period jobs in [S2] are not operating staff.

costs.priceBasis: 2012 USD (project financed 2012), reported capital cost of the desalination plant only; total project with pipeline, financing and SDCWA works $1.003B

provenance.note: constructionTotal: [S2] IDE Americas 2015 'Total Capital Cost' table: total desalination plant $537 million; total conveyance pipeline $159 million; financing costs $227 million; Water Authority improvements and oversight $80 million; total capital costs $1.003 billion. [S1] SDCWA also refers to 'the $537 million plant' and 'the $159 million pipeline'. [S2] dates financial close and notice to proceed to 2012. Operating cost, electricity price and water price are left blank because no source gives the plant's operating cost. The 2016 SDCWA water purchase price in [S2] ($2,131 to $2,367 per acre-foot, including the pipeline) is a wholesale price that includes capital recovery, so it is not an operating cost.

notes: Flows are per-day figures spread evenly over 24 hours (operatingHoursPerDay = 24), because the plant runs continuously.
